Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves that later turn black and scabby. Infected leaves may curl, pucker and drop early. Fruit develops corky, scabbed lesions.
treatment: Remove and destroy fallen leaves in autumn, since the fungus overwinters in leaf litter.
Apply a protectant fungicide (captan or myclobutanil) starting at bud break, repeating every 7-10 days through wet spring weather.
Prune to open the canopy so foliage dries faster after rain.
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties where possible.
Rake and dispose of fallen leaves every autumn.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the soil line.

Apple___Black_rot.symptoms: Purple-bordered brown spots on leaves that enlarge with concentric rings (frog-eye leaf spot). Fruit develops firm brown rot with concentric black rings, often starting at the calyx end.
treatment: Prune out dead or cankered wood, cutting well below visible discoloration.
Remove mummified fruit left on the tree or ground, which harbors spores.
Apply a fungicide labeled for black rot during the growing season.
prevention: Maintain tree vigor; the fungus favors stressed or wounded wood.
Sanitize pruning cuts and disinfect tools between trees.
Remove nearby dead wood and brush piles that can host the fungus.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface that enlarge over the season, with tube-like structures forming on the underside later in summer.
treatment: Apply a protectant fungicide from pink bud stage through several weeks after petal fall.
Remove nearby juniper or cedar trees within a few hundred meters if feasible, since the fungus needs both hosts to complete its cycle.
Rake and destroy fallen infected leaves.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars.
Avoid planting apples near ornamental junipers.
Monitor nearby cedars for orange gelatinous galls in spring, the fungus's other life stage.

Apple___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green colour, no spots, scabbing, or rust pustules. Leaf margins intact.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Maintain a regular fungicide schedule during wet spring weather in scab-prone areas.
Prune annually for airflow and remove fallen leaves each autumn.

Blueberry___healthy.symptoms: Firm green leaves with no spotting, mottling or premature reddening outside of normal autumn colour change.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Maintain acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5) which blueberries require for healthy growth.
Ensure good drainage; blueberries are sensitive to waterlogged roots.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White powdery fungal growth on leaf surfaces and shoot tips, often starting on the youngest leaves. Leaves may curl or twist.
treatment: Apply sulfur-based or potassium bicarbonate fungicide at first sign of white patches.
Prune out and destroy heavily infected shoots.
Improve air circulation by thinning dense canopy growth.
prevention: Choose resistant rootstock and cultivars where available.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth mildew favors.
Space trees for good airflow.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.symptoms: Smooth, uniformly green leaves with no white powdery patches or distortion.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Monitor for early powdery mildew symptoms in warm, humid weather.
Prune for airflow annually.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.symptoms: Rectangular tan to gray lesions running parallel to leaf veins, often with a yellow halo. Lesions can merge and cause significant leaf blighting.
treatment: Apply a foliar fungicide (strobilurin or triazole class) if disease pressure is high, particularly on susceptible hybrids.
Rotate away from corn for at least one season if the field has a history of gray leaf spot.
Consider tillage to bury infected residue where gray leaf spot has been severe.
prevention: Select resistant hybrids, the most effective long-term control.
Rotate crops away from corn and manage residue.
Avoid excessive plant density, which increases humidity in the canopy.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.symptoms: Small, cinnamon-brown, elongated pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces, which rupture and release rust-colored spores.
treatment: Apply a fungicide if rust develops before tasseling on susceptible hybrids, since yield loss is greatest with early infection.
Most modern hybrids have adequate resistance and require no treatment for typical infection levels.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrids, which is the primary control method.
Monitor fields during cool, humid weather when rust develops fastest.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Long, elliptical, gray-green to tan lesions resembling cigar shapes, running parallel to the leaf midrib. Lesions can coalesce and blight large areas of leaf.
treatment: Apply a foliar fungicide at first sign of lesions if the hybrid is susceptible and weather remains favorable for disease (cool, wet).
Rotate away from corn where the disease has been severe, since the fungus survives in residue.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids where northern leaf blight is a recurring problem.
Manage crop residue through tillage or rotation.
Scout fields regularly starting at tasseling.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green colour along the full leaf length, no lesions, pustules, or discoloration.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Rotate corn with non-host crops such as soybean.
Select hybrids with resistance ratings appropriate to local disease pressure.

Grape___Black_rot.symptoms: Small tan spots with dark borders on leaves, and small black fruiting bodies visible within older lesions. Infected berries shrivel into hard black mummies.
treatment: Apply a fungicide program starting at bud break and continuing through fruit set, since this is the most critical infection period.
Remove mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning.
Improve canopy airflow through leaf pulling and shoot thinning.
prevention: Prune out and destroy all mummified fruit and infected wood each winter.
Choose a training system that promotes airflow and sun exposure.
Avoid planting in low-lying, poorly ventilated sites.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).pathogen: Complex of fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern of yellow and brown discoloration between leaf veins. Berries may show small dark spots (measles). Symptoms often appear suddenly in mid-summer.
treatment: There is no curative fungicide treatment once wood is infected; management is preventive.
Remove and destroy severely affected vines or canes to reduce inoculum.
Protect pruning wounds with a wound sealant, since infection typically enters through cuts.
prevention: Prune during dry weather when possible, since wet conditions favor infection through wounds.
Avoid large pruning cuts where feasible; use double pruning in high-risk regions.
Maintain vine vigor to slow disease progression.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.symptoms: Angular, reddish-brown spots on leaves that can merge into larger blighted areas, sometimes causing premature defoliation.
treatment: Apply a protectant fungicide during warm, wet periods when the disease is active.
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves at the end of the season.
prevention: Prune for good canopy airflow to reduce leaf wetness duration.
Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day.
Practice good sanitation by clearing fallen leaf debris.

Grape___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green leaf colour with no spotting, striping, or fruiting bodies visible.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Maintain an appropriate fungicide program through the growing season in disease-prone regions.
Practice good canopy management for airflow.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter spp. (bacteria, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid)
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetric yellow mottling on leaves that does not follow the leaf vein pattern (unlike nutrient deficiency). Fruit is small, lopsided, and bitter, with green colour persisting at the stem end.
treatment: There is no cure. Infected trees should be removed and destroyed to prevent the disease spreading to healthy trees.
Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector with approved insecticides to slow spread within a grove.
Report suspected cases to local agricultural authorities, since this disease is often subject to quarantine regulation.
prevention: Source only certified disease-free nursery stock.
Monitor and control psyllid populations proactively.
Remove infected trees promptly rather than attempting to nurse them, since they act as a source of further spread.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown and often fall out, leaving a shot-hole appearance. Fruit develops sunken, cracked lesions.
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericide sprays during dormancy and early season, since options for active infection are limited.
Avoid working among wet trees, which spreads bacteria via water and contact.
Prune out severely affected shoots.
prevention: Plant less susceptible peach varieties where available.
Avoid overhead irrigation and excessive nitrogen, both of which favor disease development.
Maintain good airflow through pruning.

Peach___healthy.symptoms: Smooth, uniformly green leaves with no water-soaked spots or shot-hole damage.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Apply preventive copper sprays during dormancy in regions where bacterial spot is common.
Avoid wetting foliage during irrigation.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo, that can merge and cause leaf drop. Fruit develops raised, scabby spots.
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides, ideally combined with mancozeb, which slows resistance development.
Remove and destroy severely infected plants to reduce bacterial spread.
Avoid overhead watering and working among wet plants.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants.
Rotate away from peppers and tomatoes for at least one year.
Space plants for airflow and avoid overhead irrigation.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green colour with no water-soaked spotting or scabby lesions.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Use disease-free seed and rotate crops.
Avoid overhead irrigation and handling wet plants.

Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric target-like rings on older leaves first, often with a yellow halo. Severe infection causes premature defoliation.
treatment: Apply a protectant fungicide (chlorothalonil or mancozeb) on a 7-10 day schedule once symptoms appear.
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves.
Ensure adequate soil fertility, since stressed plants are more susceptible.
prevention: Rotate potatoes with non-solanaceous crops for at least two seasons.
Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day.
Maintain balanced fertilization, especially nitrogen and potassium.

Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large, water-soaked, dark green to brown lesions on leaves, often with white fuzzy growth on the underside in humid conditions. Spreads extremely fast and can destroy a crop within days.
treatment: Act immediately, since this disease spreads faster than almost any other potato disease.
Remove and destroy infected plants entirely, not just affected leaves.
Apply a systemic or protectant fungicide to remaining healthy plants without delay.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes.
Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles, which harbor the pathogen between seasons.
Avoid overhead irrigation and monitor closely during cool, wet weather.

Potato___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green foliage with no lesions, target spots, or water-soaked patches.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Rotate crops and use certified seed potatoes.
Monitor closely during cool, wet weather when late blight risk is highest.

Raspberry___healthy.symptoms: Firm green leaves with no spotting, rust pustules, or distortion.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Prune out old canes after fruiting to maintain airflow.
Space plants adequately to reduce humidity within the canopy.

Soybean___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green trifoliate leaves with no spotting, mosaic pattern, or curling.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Rotate with non-host crops such as corn.
Select varieties with resistance appropriate to local disease pressure.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White, powdery fungal patches on the upper and lower leaf surface, starting on older leaves and spreading rapidly. Severe infection causes leaves to yellow and die.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, or a labeled synthetic) at first sign of white patches.
Remove heavily infected leaves to slow spread.
Improve airflow by thinning dense foliage.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties where available.
Space plants for airflow and avoid overcrowding.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which promotes susceptible new growth.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Small, irregular purple spots on leaves that enlarge and merge, giving leaves a scorched, reddish-brown appearance. Severe infection reduces plant vigor and yield.
treatment: Apply a labeled fungicide during wet spring weather when the disease is most active.
Remove infected leaves after harvest to reduce overwintering spores.
Renovate beds after fruiting by mowing old foliage.
prevention: Plant resistant strawberry varieties where available.
Space plants for airflow and avoid overhead irrigation.
Remove old infected foliage each season.

Strawberry___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green leaves with no purple spotting or scorched margins.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Maintain good airflow and avoid overhead watering.
Renovate beds after fruiting each season.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, often ringed by a yellow halo, that turn brown to black. Fruit develops raised, scabby lesions.
treatment: Apply copper-based sprays to slow the spread; they do not cure infected tissue.
Remove severely infected plants to reduce bacterial load.
Never work among wet plants, since bacteria spread readily by contact.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants.
Rotate crops for at least one year away from tomato and pepper.
Sanitize stakes, ties and tools between plants.

Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown lesions with concentric rings resembling a target, usually starting on the oldest lowest leaves and moving upward.
treatment: Remove and destroy affected lower leaves as soon as lesions appear.
Apply a protectant fungicide (chlorothalonil or mancozeb) every 7-10 days during wet weather.
Mulch around plants to stop rain splashing spores from soil onto foliage.
prevention: Rotate tomatoes with non-solanaceous crops for two to three seasons.
Space and stake plants for good airflow.
Clear plant debris at the end of the season.

Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large, greasy, grey-green to brown blotches on leaves, often with white fuzzy growth on the underside in humid conditions. Spreads extremely fast.
treatment: Act immediately, since this disease can destroy a crop within days.
Remove and destroy infected plants entirely; do not leave debris in the field.
Apply a protectant fungicide (mancozeb, chlorothalonil, or copper) to remaining healthy plants.
prevention: Avoid planting near infected potato crops, which share the same pathogen.
Monitor closely during cool, wet weather when risk is highest.
Stop overhead irrigation if an outbreak is suspected nearby.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green to yellow patches on the upper leaf surface, with olive-green to grayish-purple fuzzy mold visible on the underside directly beneath. Common in humid greenhouse conditions.
treatment: Improve ventilation and reduce humidity around plants immediately, since this disease thrives in still, humid air.
Apply a labeled fungicide if humidity cannot be reduced sufficiently.
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves.
prevention: Space plants well and prune for airflow, especially in greenhouses or tunnels.
Avoid overhead watering and water early in the day so foliage dries quickly.
Choose resistant varieties where available.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark brown margins and pale gray centers, often with tiny black fruiting bodies visible in the center. Usually starts on lower leaves.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves promptly.
Apply a protectant fungicide (chlorothalonil or copper) on a regular schedule during wet weather.
Mulch to prevent soil splash onto foliage.
prevention: Rotate away from tomato for at least one season.
Stake plants and remove lower leaves that touch the soil.
Water at the soil line rather than overhead.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine yellow stippling or speckling on leaves, sometimes with fine webbing visible on the underside or between leaves in heavy infestations. Leaves may bronze and dry out.
treatment: Spray plants with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites, effective for light infestations.
Apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, targeting the underside of leaves where mites live.
For heavy infestations, use a labeled miticide, rotating chemical classes to avoid resistance.
prevention: Avoid drought stress, which makes plants more attractive to mites.
Encourage natural predators such as predatory mites and lacewings.
Avoid excessive dust, which favors mite reproduction; hose down foliage periodically in dry weather.

Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric target-like rings, similar to early blight but often larger and found throughout the plant rather than just lower leaves. Can also affect stems and fruit.
treatment: Apply a protectant fungicide labeled for target spot on a regular schedule during warm, wet weather.
Remove and destroy severely infected leaves.
Improve airflow through pruning and adequate spacing.
prevention: Rotate away from tomato and related crops.
Avoid overhead irrigation and prolonged leaf wetness.
Remove plant debris at the end of the season.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaves, stunted growth, and reduced fruit set. Leaves are often smaller than normal with a distinctive cupped, crinkled appearance.
treatment: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy infected plants to reduce virus reservoir.
Control whitefly populations aggressively with insecticidal soap, neem oil, or labeled insecticides, since whiteflies are the sole vector.
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce whitefly numbers.
prevention: Plant virus-resistant tomato varieties where available.
Use reflective mulch, which disrupts whitefly landing behaviour.
Remove weeds near the growing area, which can harbor both whiteflies and the virus.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.pathogen: Tobamovirus, spread by contact and contaminated tools
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves, sometimes with leaf distortion, curling, or fern-like narrowing. Fruit may show internal browning.
treatment: There is no cure; remove and destroy infected plants promptly to prevent spread.
Wash hands and disinfect tools thoroughly after handling infected plants, since the virus spreads easily by contact.
Avoid using tobacco products near plants, since a related virus can cross-contaminate.
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties where available.
Disinfect tools, stakes and hands between plants as routine practice.
Control weeds that can harbor the virus between seasons.

Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Uniformly medium to dark green leaf with firm, turgid tissue and no spotting, yellowing, curling, or necrotic margins.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Rotate crops and maintain balanced fertilization.
Monitor regularly for early signs of the diseases common in your region.

Apple_fruit___Blotch.pathogen: Botryosphaeria obtusa or Colletotrichum spp. (fungal complex)
Apple_fruit___Blotch.symptoms: Dark, irregular, olive-to-black blotches on the fruit skin that enlarge and merge, often with a slightly sunken or rough texture. Frequently develops on fruit close to harvest.
treatment: Remove and discard visibly blotched fruit; do not store it with healthy fruit since the fungus spreads in storage.
Apply a fungicide programme (captan or a strobilurin) during the growing season, timed to cover the pre-harvest period.
Improve air circulation around fruit by thinning dense canopy growth.
prevention: Prune out dead or cankered wood each dormant season, which harbours the fungus over winter.
Harvest promptly at maturity rather than leaving fruit on the tree.
Avoid bruising fruit during picking and handling, since wounds are common infection points.

Apple_fruit___Rot.pathogen: Botryosphaeria and Colletotrichum species (bitter rot complex)
Apple_fruit___Rot.symptoms: Soft, sunken, circular brown lesions on the fruit surface that expand concentrically, sometimes with visible spore masses in the centre under humid conditions.
treatment: Discard rotted fruit immediately; it is not safe to eat and will spread spores to sound fruit in storage.
Apply a protective fungicide programme through summer, particularly after wounding events like hail or insect damage.
Cool harvested fruit promptly, since rot develops fastest at warm storage temperatures.
prevention: Remove mummified fruit and dead wood from the orchard each winter.
Handle fruit carefully to avoid the small wounds that let the fungus enter.
Store fruit at low temperature and inspect regularly, removing any rotting fruit at once.

Apple_fruit___Scab.symptoms: Rough, corky, olive-to-brown scabbed patches on the fruit skin, often with cracking as the fruit expands. The same fungus that causes leaf scab.
treatment: Fruit already scabbed cannot be cured; the goal is to protect the remaining crop.
Apply a protectant fungicide (captan or myclobutanil) starting at bloom and continuing through early summer.
Remove and destroy fallen leaves in autumn, since the fungus overwinters there and reinfects fruit the following season.
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties where replanting is an option.
Rake and dispose of fallen leaves every autumn without exception.
Prune for an open canopy so fruit and foliage dry quickly after rain.

Apple_fruit___healthy.symptoms: Smooth, evenly coloured skin with no blotching, rot, or scabbed patches.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Maintain a preventive fungicide schedule through the growing season in disease-prone regions.
Harvest promptly and handle fruit gently to avoid wounds that invite infection.

Guava_fruit___Anthracnose.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on the fruit that enlarge into sunken, dark brown to black lesions, often with pink spore masses visible in humid weather. Commonly appears as fruit ripens.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected fruit; the fungus spreads readily to sound fruit in storage.
Apply a copper-based or systemic fungicide during flowering and fruit development, particularly in wet seasons.
Harvest fruit promptly at maturity rather than allowing overripening on the tree.
prevention: Prune to improve airflow through the canopy, which reduces the humidity the fungus needs.
Remove mummified fruit and fallen debris from under trees.
Avoid wounding fruit during harvest and handling.

Guava_fruit___Fruitfly.symptoms: Small puncture marks on the skin where eggs were laid, with the flesh beneath turning soft, discoloured and often infested with larvae. Affected fruit may drop prematurely.
treatment: Remove and destroy infested fruit promptly, including any that has dropped, to break the fly's life cycle.
Use protein-bait traps or approved insecticide bait stations to reduce the adult fly population.
Bag developing fruit on the tree with fine mesh or paper bags to physically block egg-laying.
prevention: Maintain orchard sanitation by collecting and destroying fallen fruit weekly during the season.
Time harvest to pick fruit slightly under-ripe, since flies preferentially target fully ripe fruit.
Monitor with pheromone or bait traps to catch population increases early.

Guava_fruit___healthy.symptoms: Firm, evenly coloured skin with no sunken lesions, puncture marks, or soft spots.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Maintain orchard sanitation and monitor for fruit fly activity through the season.
Harvest at the right maturity stage and handle fruit gently.

Mango_fruit___Alternaria.symptoms: Circular, dark brown to black lesions on the fruit surface, often starting near the stem end, with the flesh beneath turning soft and discoloured as the rot progresses.
treatment: Discard affected fruit; do not store with healthy fruit as spores spread easily.
Apply a post-harvest fungicide dip where permitted, and ensure fruit is dry before storage.
Reduce field infection with a fungicide programme during late fruit development.
prevention: Harvest fruit at the correct maturity and avoid mechanical injury during picking.
Store fruit at recommended cool temperatures to slow fungal development.
Remove and destroy mummified fruit left on the tree after harvest.

Mango_fruit___Anthracnose.symptoms: Small dark spots that enlarge into irregular black, sunken lesions, frequently appearing as fruit ripens after harvest. Severely affected fruit may show cracking and premature rotting.
treatment: Discard visibly affected fruit promptly.
Apply pre-harvest fungicide sprays during flowering and fruit development, which is the most effective control window.
Use hot water treatment after harvest where facilities allow, which suppresses latent infections.
prevention: Prune for good airflow and sunlight penetration through the canopy.
Avoid harvesting during or immediately after rain, when spore spread is highest.
Remove and destroy fallen leaves and mummified fruit, which harbour the fungus.

Mango_fruit___Black_mould_rot.symptoms: Dark, powdery fungal growth developing on damaged or overripe fruit, typically starting at wounds or the stem end and spreading across the surface with a soft, rotted texture beneath.
treatment: Remove and discard affected fruit immediately, since Aspergillus can produce mycotoxins.
Handle remaining fruit carefully to avoid the wounds that allow this mould to establish.
Store fruit at correct cool, dry conditions rather than warm humid storage.
prevention: Avoid bruising or puncturing fruit during harvest, transport, and storage.
Cure or dry any surface wounds promptly and keep storage areas clean and well ventilated.
Discard overripe fruit before mould has a chance to establish.

Mango_fruit___Stem_end_rot.symptoms: Dark brown to black rot beginning at the stem attachment point and spreading downward into the fruit, often accompanied by a shrivelled, sunken appearance around the stem.
treatment: Discard fruit showing stem-end darkening; the rot spreads quickly through the flesh.
Apply a post-harvest fungicide treatment at the stem end where available.
Ensure fruit is harvested with an intact stem stub rather than pulled or snapped.
prevention: Harvest with clean, sharp tools leaving a short stem stub to reduce the wound size at the point of infection.
Avoid delays between harvest and cooling, since warm conditions accelerate the rot.
Remove dead wood and mummified fruit from trees, which are a source of spores.

Mango_fruit___healthy.symptoms: Smooth, evenly coloured skin with no dark lesions, sunken spots, or rot at the stem end.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Handle fruit gently and harvest with an intact stem stub.
Store at recommended cool temperatures and inspect regularly.

Orange_fruit___Black_spot.pathogen: Phyllosticta citricarpa (fungus, also called citrus black spot)
Orange_fruit___Black_spot.symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark margins and grey-brown centres scattered across the peel, sometimes surrounded by a yellow halo. Mainly a cosmetic disease affecting fruit appearance.
treatment: Apply a protectant fungicide programme through summer, since black spot cannot be treated once lesions appear.
Remove fallen leaves and fruit debris under trees, which is where the fungus overwinters.
Prune to improve airflow and reduce leaf wetness duration.
prevention: Maintain a preventive fungicide schedule in regions where black spot is established.
Practise orchard sanitation by removing fallen leaf litter regularly.
Consider resistant or less-susceptible citrus varieties where replanting is an option.

Orange_fruit___Canker.symptoms: Raised, corky, brown lesions on the fruit surface with a water-soaked yellow halo, often circular with a crater-like centre. Highly contagious between trees.
treatment: There is no cure for infected fruit; affected fruit should be removed and destroyed.
Apply copper-based bactericide sprays to protect remaining healthy fruit, particularly after wind or rain events.
Avoid working among wet trees, since the bacteria spread easily via water and contact.
prevention: Use disease-free planting material and inspect new stock carefully before planting.
Windbreaks reduce wind-driven rain, a major spread mechanism.
Report suspected outbreaks to local agricultural authorities, since canker is often subject to quarantine control.

Orange_fruit___Greening.pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter spp. (bacteria, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid)
Orange_fruit___Greening.symptoms: Fruit remains small, lopsided, and green at the stem end even when otherwise ripe, often with a bitter, unpleasant taste. Seeds inside may be dark and aborted.
treatment: There is no cure. Infected trees should be removed and destroyed to prevent the disease spreading further.
Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector with approved insecticides to slow spread within a grove.
Report suspected cases to local agricultural authorities, since this disease is often subject to quarantine regulation.
prevention: Source only certified disease-free nursery stock.
Monitor and control psyllid populations proactively.
Remove infected trees promptly rather than attempting to nurse them, since they act as a source of further spread.

Orange_fruit___healthy.symptoms: Evenly coloured, firm peel with no raised lesions, corky spots, or abnormal green patches at maturity.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Monitor for psyllid activity and canker symptoms through the season.
Maintain orchard sanitation and a preventive fungicide programme where black spot is present locally.

Pomegranate_fruit___Alternaria.symptoms: Dark brown to black irregular spots on the fruit rind, which may enlarge and cause the surface beneath to rot. Often develops on fruit already stressed by sunburn or cracking.
treatment: Remove and discard affected fruit promptly.
Apply a protective fungicide programme during fruit development, particularly in humid weather.
Reduce fruit cracking and sunburn through adequate irrigation and canopy shade, since wounded fruit is more susceptible.
prevention: Maintain even soil moisture to reduce fruit cracking, a common entry point for this fungus.
Prune to provide some canopy shade over fruit in very hot climates.
Remove fallen and mummified fruit from the orchard floor.

Pomegranate_fruit___Anthracnose.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots that develop into sunken, dark brown to black lesions, sometimes with visible pink spore masses in humid conditions. Fruit may crack and rot as the disease progresses.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected fruit; the fungus spreads readily to healthy fruit nearby.
Apply a fungicide programme during flowering and early fruit development.
Improve airflow through pruning to reduce the humidity the fungus needs to spread.
prevention: Practise field sanitation by removing fallen fruit and dead wood regularly.
Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps fruit surfaces wet for extended periods.
Harvest promptly at maturity rather than leaving fruit to overripen on the tree.

Pomegranate_fruit___Bacterial_blight.symptoms: Irregular, dark, water-soaked lesions on the fruit surface that later turn brown to black, often with cracking of the rind. A serious disease that can also affect leaves and stems.
treatment: Remove and destroy severely affected fruit and prune out infected twigs.
Apply copper-based bactericide sprays, particularly during and after rainy periods when spread is fastest.
Avoid working among wet plants, since the bacteria spread readily by water and contact.
prevention: Use disease-free planting material from a reputable source.
Sanitise pruning tools between plants to avoid spreading the bacteria mechanically.
Avoid overhead irrigation and manage orchard drainage to reduce prolonged wetness.

Pomegranate_fruit___Cercospora.symptoms: Small, circular to irregular brown spots on the fruit rind, sometimes with a greyish centre, which can merge into larger blotched areas on heavily affected fruit.
treatment: Remove and destroy fruit with extensive spotting.
Apply a fungicide programme during fruit development in humid growing seasons.
Improve canopy airflow through pruning to reduce leaf and fruit wetness duration.
prevention: Practise field sanitation by removing fallen leaves and fruit debris.
Avoid dense planting that restricts airflow through the canopy.
Monitor closely during warm, humid weather when the disease develops fastest.

Pomegranate_fruit___healthy.symptoms: Smooth, evenly coloured rind with no dark spotting, cracking, or lesions.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring.
prevention: Maintain even soil moisture to reduce fruit cracking.
Practise field sanitation and monitor during humid weather for early disease signs.
